source: What Modern Orthodox families in the United States report spending on a bar or bat mitzvah, a year in Israel, a wedding and the first years of a young couple, gathered in summer 2026 and rounded to bands.
confidenceNote: A simcha costs what a family decides it costs. The bands are wide on purpose; the planner asks for the family's own figure and uses the typical one only until it has it.

events.label: Bar mitzvah
events.note: Tefillin and the lessons, the kiddush, the seudah or party, and the trip if there is one.

events.label: Bat mitzvah
events.note: The celebration, the chesed project, the trip if there is one.

events.label: The year in Israel
events.note: Counted on the tuition page when the child's gap year is on. It shows here so the timeline is whole.

events.label: Wedding
events.note: The whole wedding. Below, the share convention says how much of it is yours.

events.label: Supporting the young couple
events.note: A year of help while they study or start out. The planner multiplies by the number of years you expect to give it.

weddingShares.label: FLOP
weddingShares.note: The chatan's family pays flowers, liquor, orchestra and photography; the kallah's family pays the rest. Roughly a third to two thirds.

aliyah.label: Aliyah

items.label: The first three months
items.note: Rent and deposits, a car, appliances, ulpan, the school's absorption fees.

aliyah.note: Nefesh B'Nefesh and the Jewish Agency give grants and the flight; the Ministry of Absorption pays a living stipend for the first months. A new oleh's foreign income and assets are exempt from Israeli tax for ten years, though reporting rules changed in 2026. Check both before you count on them.
